summary: Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate (TI-LFA) is a fast reroute method for Segment Routing. It precomputes backup paths so traffic can be switched quickly around a failed link or node, protecting node and adjacency segments. It builds on earlier IP fast reroute ideas such as LFA and remote LFA.

plainLanguage.summary: A good driver already knows a backup road before the main road gets blocked. Routers do the same, so traffic can swerve in an instant when something breaks.

questions: what is the post-convergence path in fast reroute
subtitle: Precomputed backup paths for Segment Routing that follow where traffic would go after the network reconverges.

tldr.problem: Older fast reroute methods (LFA and remote LFA) cannot protect every destination in every topology, and they leave operators tuning tie-breaks between backup options.
tldr.mechanism: The router next to the failure precomputes, for each destination, a backup path along the expected post-convergence path and encodes it as a short list of Segment Routing segments, using the P-space and Q-space ideas from remote LFA.
tldr.outcome: TI-LFA gives guaranteed coverage in any two-connected network running a link-state IGP, for single link, node or SRLG failures, without extra tunnel sessions or per-path state in the network.

today: RFC 9855 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025, and the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the LFA and remote LFA work in RFC 5286 and RFC 7490 and relies on the Segment Routing architecture in RFC 8402.

sections.title: Why Another Fast Reroute Method
sections.content:
RFC 9855 describes a local repair mechanism that uses Segment Routing (SR) to restore end-to-end connectivity after a failure of a directly connected link, node or Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG). It is meant for standard link-state IGP shortest path scenarios. Non-SR local repair is out of scope, and non-local failures are handled in a separate document.

The Topology Independent in the name means the loop-free backup path works across all network topologies. The RFC contrasts this with RFC 5286 (LFA) and RFC 7490 (remote LFA), which cannot give complete protection coverage in some topologies, as described in RFC 6571.

Because all the Segment Identifiers (SIDs) needed are already in the IGP link state database, TI-LFA does not need targeted LDP sessions to remote nodes, and it adds no extra state in the network to force explicit backup paths. Its scope is limited to protecting links, nodes and SRLGs inside one link-state IGP area.
sections.plainLanguage: Older backup plans sometimes had no answer for certain road maps. This one always finds a safe detour, as long as the map has at least two ways around.

sections.title: Key Terms: PLR, P-space and Q-space
sections.content:
The Point of Local Repair (PLR) is the router that switches traffic quickly after it detects a failure on a directly attached link, set of links or neighbor node. TI-LFA works out the backup path at the PLR, so no coordination or message exchange with other routers is needed.

The RFC reuses two ideas from RFC 7490. The P-space of a router with regard to a failed resource X is the set of routers it can reach on pre-convergence shortest paths that do not pass through X. The Q-space is the set of routers that can reach the destination without any path passing through X. A node in both is a PQ node. The extended P-space is the union of the P-spaces of the PLR's neighbors that are not reached using X.

The PLR protects in one of three modes: link failure, node failure (the neighbor on the primary link is assumed to have failed), or SRLG failure (a configured set of links sharing fate with the primary link).
sections.plainLanguage: Picture a town map. Some places you can still reach without using the broken bridge, and some places can still reach your destination without it. A good detour goes through places that do both.

sections.title: Building the Repair Path
sections.content:
The base idea is to precompute the shortest path tree as it would look after the failure, then encode the expected post-convergence path to each destination as a loop-free list of segments called the Repair List (RL). The simplest encoding is a list of Adjacency SIDs only, but that can be too long for hardware because of Maximum SID Depth limits. Combining Node-SIDs and Adjacency SIDs shortens it, and using Node-SIDs lets traffic use equal-cost multipath on the backup path.

Implementations MAY intersect the P-space, extended P-space and Q-space with the nodes on the post-convergence path. The general form of the result is (Node-SID(P), EP(P, Q)), where EP(P, Q) is an explicit SR path from a P node to a Q node. The RFC says finding the best trade-off between scaling and accuracy of the Q-space computation is up to each implementation.

The RFC then describes four shapes of repair, each comparable to an older technique: a direct neighbor (empty RL), a single PQ node, a P node and an adjacent Q node, and distant P and Q nodes connected by a list of segments. How the shortest list is found in the last case is left to the implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: The router writes down the whole detour as a short list of stops: go to this town first, then take these roads. The shorter the list, the easier it is for the router to remember.

sections.title: Applying the Repair List to Packets
sections.content:
When the primary outgoing interface fails, the protecting router S must handle the packet's active segment according to its type.

  • Node segment: the active segment MUST be kept unchanged and the RL MUST be added in front of it.
  • Adjacency segment followed by another Adjacency segment: S MUST apply a NEXT operation on the Adj-SID, then one or more PUSH operations so the packet reaches F. If the RL ends at F, only the RL is pushed. Otherwise a node segment of F is pushed first, followed by the RL.
  • Adjacency segment followed by a node segment: S MUST apply NEXT and then push an RL that redirects traffic to a node Q whose path to that node segment is not affected by the failure.

For a protected Adjacency segment, the RFC says merging back at the remote end keeps as much traffic as possible on the pre-failure path. When SR policies need strict compliance, end-to-end protection should be preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: When the road is blocked, the router tacks the detour directions onto the front of the packet's own directions. Once the detour is done, the packet carries on with its original plan.

sections.title: SR-MPLS and SRv6 Data Planes
sections.content:
The path computation is the same for both data planes, but pushing the RL differs. For SR-MPLS, if the active segment is a node segment signaled with penultimate hop popping and the RL ends with an Adjacency segment terminating on the penultimate node, the active segment MUST be popped before pushing the RL. Otherwise the active segment MUST be popped and pushed again with a label computed from the Segment Routing Global Block (SRGB) of Q, the endpoint of the RL, and then the RL MUST be pushed.

For SRv6, Adjacency SIDs are typically globally routed, so they need no preceding Prefix-SID and the RL is likely shorter. At a transit node an SRv6 SID list is added following the head-end behaviors of RFC 8986. At a Segment Endpoint node, the endpoint processing runs first and the packet is then protected as if it were transit traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Different kinds of road signs need slightly different ways of pinning the detour note on the packet, but the detour itself is worked out the same way.

sections.title: Flexible Algorithms, Adjacency SIDs and Post-Convergence Paths
sections.content:
Segment Routing lets an operator bind an algorithm to a Prefix-SID. With the default algorithm, local policies can override the IGP shortest path, so there is no guarantee the TI-LFA path is loop-free. The RFC makes it the operator's responsibility to ensure such policies do not affect TI-LFA, and notes this can already happen with RLFA. An implementation MAY support TI-LFA for Node-SIDs of a Flexible Algorithm (RFC 9350); it SHOULD then use the constrained SPF of that algorithm in all computations, and SHOULD only use SIDs bound to it, or unprotected Adj-SIDs of the regular SPF, to build the RL.

An RL can contain Adjacency segments that are themselves protected. If one fails during FRR, a second repair activates. An implementation MAY avoid this by picking only unprotected Adjacency segments. The RFC adds that FRR protects a single pre-planned failure and fast IGP convergence remains important.

Appendix A explains why following the expected post-convergence path reduces the need for local backup-selection policies (RFC 7916) and matches common capacity planning. It also warns that a node-protecting path is used even if only a link actually failed, and that TI-LFA cannot know the constraints of an SR policy (RFC 9256), so such policies should compute their own backup rather than rely on local protection.
sections.plainLanguage: A detour only works if everyone follows the usual road rules. The RFC reminds operators not to change the rules in ways that break the detour, and says a backup plan only covers one problem at a time.

sections.title: Measurements on Real Networks
sections.content:
Appendix B reports an analysis on nine real service provider and large enterprise topologies (T1 to T9, from 34 to 587 nodes). For each network the algorithms were applied to protect all prefixes against link, node and local SRLG failure, and the number of SIDs in each repair path was recorded. The counts apply to SR over MPLS.

The RFC summarizes the result this way: for link and local SRLG protection, a repair path of 1 SID or less gives more than 99% coverage, and for node protection a repair path of 2 SIDs or less yields 99%. A repair with 0 SIDs corresponds to a direct neighbor that is also a loop-free alternate, and 1 SID to a PQ node.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors tried the idea on real maps of big networks. Almost every detour turned out to need only a very short list of directions.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The techniques are internal functions of a router that guarantee an upper bound on the time taken to restore traffic after a directly connected link or node fails. Steering traffic to the post-convergence path quickly minimizes disruption, which the RFC calls a modest security enhancement. The mechanism protects destinations inside a routing domain, not external ones.

The security considerations of RFC 5286, RFC 7490, RFC 8402 and the SR data plane documents apply. The document states that it introduces no additional security concerns. It has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a router fixing its own traffic quickly, not a new way for outsiders to talk to it, so it adds no new risks.

PCPath                 = <N2 -> R1 -> R2 -> R3 -> D>
P node chosen          = R1
Q node chosen          = R3
